Deep learning · chapter 2.7 · autoencoders & VAEs

Autoencoders & VAEs

Squeeze an image into two numbers, then learn to dream

An autoencoder is a network trained to copy its input through a narrow middle. To get the copy right it has to find a short description of the data, a code. A variational autoencoder goes further: it arranges those codes into a smooth map that you can sample from, so its decoder can draw things it has never seen. On the right, every dot is a handwritten test digit, placed by a VAE that keeps only two numbers per image. Move your pointer over the map (or drag a finger): the decoder draws the digit that lives at each spot, including spots where no real digit sits.

The idea
Compress to a small code, then rebuild; the code must keep what matters
The VAE twist
Encode each input as a little Gaussian cloud, and keep the clouds near N(0, I)
In practice
Compression, denoising, anomaly detection, and the image latents inside Stable Diffusion

The idea

Squeeze through a bottleneck

An autoencoder is two networks back to back. The encoder f turns an input x into a short code z; the decoder g tries to rebuild x from z alone. If z were as wide as x, the pair could simply learn to copy and would learn nothing. The narrow middle, the bottleneck, forces a choice: keep what is needed to rebuild the data, drop the rest. No labels are involved; the input is its own target, which is why this is called self-supervised learning.

Below, 150 points lie near a curve in a plane: two numbers each. The bottleneck is one number. Each point is drawn with a line to its reconstruction, coloured by its code. Press Train and watch the reconstructions slide onto a curve; then switch to a straight bottleneck, or to a blob that has no curve to find. Drag the ring to encode any point you like.

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{z} &= f_\phi(\mathbf{x}), \qquad \hat{\mathbf{x}} = g_\theta(\mathbf{z}) \\ \mathcal{L}(\phi, \theta) &= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \big\lVert \mathbf{x}_i - g_\theta\big(f_\phi(\mathbf{x}_i)\big) \big\rVert^2 \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: f, with weights φ, is the encoder; g, with weights θ, is the decoder. The loss is the average squared distance between each input and its own reconstruction, and both networks are trained together by gradient descent to shrink it. Here x has 2 numbers and z has 1. The curved version is 2→16→1 for the encoder and 1→16→2 for the decoder, with tanh hidden units; the straight version has no hidden layer at all.
Say it“z is f-phi of x, x-hat is g-theta of z, and the loss is the average squared distance between each x and its reconstruction.”

A familiar special case

A straight bottleneck is PCA

Take out the tanh and the autoencoder is linear: the code is z = Wx and the rebuild is Vz. Bourlard & Kamp (1988) and Baldi & Hornik (1989) proved that the best such network spans exactly the subspace of the top principal components from chapter 1.13. A linear autoencoder simply rediscovers PCA, and the toy above shows its limit: a straight line cannot follow an arc. Real digits make the point with numbers. Each MNIST image is 784 pixels. Our plain autoencoder (784→256→2→256→784, ReLU, trained offline on 60,000 digits) gets just two numbers. Slide k to give PCA more and more numbers, and find where it catches up.

\[ \begin{aligned} &\min_{W,\,V}\ \frac1n\sum_{i} \big\lVert \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_i - V W \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_i \big\rVert^2 \\ &\Rightarrow\ \operatorname{span}(V) = \operatorname{span}(\mathbf{u}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{u}_k) \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: x̃ is a digit minus the average digit. W squeezes it to k numbers and V maps them back. The best possible W and V make V’s columns span the same k directions as the top k eigenvectors u of the pixel covariance matrix: PCA. Gradient descent on a linear autoencoder finds that subspace too (though not necessarily the eigenvectors one by one).
Say it“The best linear code-and-rebuild spans the top k principal components.”
\[ \frac1n \sum_i \big\lVert \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_i - \hat{\mathbf{x}}_i \big\rVert^2 = \sum_{j > k} \lambda_j \]
Read it as: λj is the variance of the training digits along the j-th principal direction. The squared error PCA leaves behind is the variance in all the directions it throws away. Errors here are summed over the 784 pixels, with pixels running from 0 (paper) to 1 (ink).
Say it“The average squared error equals the sum of the eigenvalues beyond k.”

What the code means

The latent space: a map of digits

Two numbers are a position, so the encoder gives every digit a place on a map: the latent space. Nobody told it which digit is which (the colours were added afterwards), yet the 1s, the 0s and the 7s each settle in their own regions, because similar images need similar codes to be rebuilt well. And since the decoder accepts any pair of numbers, we can walk between two digits. Halfway between two images in pixel space is a ghostly double exposure; halfway between their codes is something that looks like handwriting. Drag the ends of the path onto two different digits, then slide t. Then drag the probe into the empty ground between the clusters.

\[ \mathbf{x}(t) = (1-t)\,\mathbf{x}_A + t\,\mathbf{x}_B \]
Read it as: blend the pixels: at t = 0.5 every pixel is the average of the two images, so you see both digits at half strength. The straight line between two images in pixel space passes through things that are not digits at all.
Say it“x of t is one-minus-t times x-A plus t times x-B.”
\[ \hat{\mathbf{x}}(t) = g_\theta\big((1-t)\,\mathbf{z}_A + t\,\mathbf{z}_B\big) \]
Read it as: blend the codes, then decode. Every frame is something the decoder knows how to draw, so the digit morphs instead of fading. The catch: on a plain autoencoder’s map the straight path may cross empty ground where no training code ever sat, and there the decoder is guessing.
Say it“x-hat of t is g of the blended code.”
code of A
code of B

The VAE, part one

Encode a cloud, not a point

The variational autoencoder (Kingma & Welling, 2014; Rezende, Mohamed & Wierstra, 2014) changes one thing in the encoder. Instead of a single point it outputs a small Gaussian cloud: a centre μ and a spread σ for each latent number. During training the decoder never sees μ itself, only a random point drawn from the cloud. So a code can no longer be a needle-thin spot that only one exact input reaches; every point near μ must decode to something close to the original digit. Clouds of similar digits overlap, and the map fills in. Click any digit to see its cloud, then draw samples from it and decode them.

\[ \begin{aligned} q_\phi(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x}) = \mathcal{N}\!\big(\mathbf{z};\ &\boldsymbol{\mu}_\phi(\mathbf{x}), \\ &\operatorname{diag}\boldsymbol{\sigma}^2_\phi(\mathbf{x})\big) \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: q is the encoder’s belief about where x’s code is: a normal distribution centred at μ(x) with spread σ(x) along each latent axis (independent axes, hence “diag”). The network actually outputs μ and log σ², two numbers per latent dimension; the log keeps σ positive without any constraint. Our VAE has the same layers as the plain autoencoder, plus a second 2-number head for log σ².
Say it“q of z given x is a normal with mean mu of x and diagonal variance sigma squared of x.”
centre μ
spread σ

The VAE, part two

The reparameterisation trick

Training needs the gradient of the loss with respect to μ and σ, but the loss depends on them through a random draw. How does a gradient pass through “pick a random number”? Kingma and Welling’s answer is to move the randomness out of the way: draw a standard normal ε first, then compute z = μ + σε. Now z is ordinary arithmetic on μ and σ, with ε as just another input, and backpropagation goes straight through. The older alternative, the score-function (REINFORCE) estimator, never differentiates the loss at all; it is unbiased too, but far noisier. To see the difference, take one latent number and a loss f(z) = (z − 2)² whose true gradient we know exactly. Change σ and the number of samples, and compare how widely each estimate scatters around the truth.

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{z} &= \boldsymbol{\mu} + \boldsymbol{\sigma} \odot \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}, \\ \boldsymbol{\varepsilon} &\sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, I) \\ \nabla_{\mu}\, \mathbb{E}\big[f(z)\big] &= \mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon}\big[f'(\mu + \sigma\varepsilon)\big] \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: ⊙ multiplies element by element. Because z is a smooth function of μ and σ for each fixed ε, the gradient of the average is the average of ordinary gradients (the pathwise estimate). Average it over N draws of ε. In a VAE this is one draw per image per step, and the batch does the averaging.
Say it“z is mu plus sigma times epsilon; the gradient of the expectation is the expectation of f-prime at mu plus sigma epsilon.”
\[ \begin{aligned} &\nabla_{\mu}\, \mathbb{E}\big[f(z)\big] \\ &= \mathbb{E}_{z \sim q}\Big[f(z)\,\frac{z-\mu}{\sigma^2}\Big] \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: the score-function estimate weights each sample’s loss by how much a shift in μ would make that sample more likely (the derivative of log q). It only needs values of f, not its slope, which is why reinforcement learning uses it (chapter 3.3). But f(z) can be large while (z − μ) flips sign at random, so the products scatter widely.
Say it“The gradient is the expectation of f of z times z minus mu over sigma squared.”
true gradient
score-function spread ÷ pathwise spread
pathwise: mean ± sd
score function: mean ± sd

The VAE, part three

The KL term: pull every cloud home

Clouds alone are not enough. Left to itself, the encoder would cheat: shrink every σ towards zero (which turns it back into a plain autoencoder) and push the centres far apart so the samples never get confused. The VAE’s loss stops this with a penalty on every cloud: its Kullback–Leibler divergence from a fixed prior, the standard normal p(z) = N(0, I). The penalty is zero only when the cloud is the prior. It grows as the centre wanders away (the μ² part) and it explodes as the cloud shrinks to a point (the −log σ² part). Move and squeeze the cloud and watch both parts.

\[ \begin{aligned} &\mathrm{KL}\big(q \,\Vert\, p\big) \\ &\quad = \mathbb{E}_{z\sim q}\big[\log q(z) - \log p(z)\big] \\ &\quad = \tfrac12 \sum_{j=1}^{d}\Big(\mu_j^2 + \sigma_j^2 - \log\sigma_j^2 - 1\Big) \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: KL measures, in nats, how much information the cloud carries beyond the prior: the average extra log-probability q gives its own samples compared with p. For two Gaussians the average has a closed form, summed over the d latent dimensions (d = 2 here). It is never negative; the μ² term pulls centres towards the origin, and σ² − log σ² − 1 is smallest, zero, at σ = 1.
Say it“KL of q from p is a half the sum of mu squared plus sigma squared minus log sigma squared minus one.”
KL, closed form (nats)
KL, 4,000 samples
½μ²: distance part
½(σ² − log σ² − 1): width part

The whole objective

The ELBO and the β dial

The VAE minimises two terms together: how badly the decoder rebuilds x from a sample of its cloud, plus the KL penalty on the cloud. This is not an arbitrary recipe. Their sum, with a minus sign, is a lower bound on log p(x), the log-probability the model assigns to the image: the evidence lower bound, or ELBO. Maximising it trains a generative model of the data, and the encoder is the helper that makes the bound tight. Higgins et al. (2017) put a knob on the balance, β, in the β-VAE. We trained five VAEs on MNIST, identical except for β. Turn the dial and watch the map and the decoded grid change.

\[ \begin{aligned} \log p_\theta(\mathbf{x}) &\ge \mathrm{ELBO} \\ \mathrm{ELBO} &= \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x})}\big[\log p_\theta(\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{z})\big]}_{-\text{reconstruction}} \\ &\quad - \underbrace{\mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x}) \,\Vert\, p(\mathbf{z})\big)}_{\text{rate}} \\ \text{loss}_\beta &= \text{reconstruction} + \beta\cdot\mathrm{KL} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: the decoder outputs a probability for every pixel to be ink (a Bernoulli decoder), so the reconstruction term is the binary cross-entropy summed over 784 pixels, in nats. The KL term is the rate: how many nats the code spends describing this particular digit. β = 1 is the true ELBO. Much smaller β buys sharper reconstructions with a sprawling, gappier map; larger β packs the map tighter and blurs the digits. All numbers below are averages over the 10,000 MNIST test digits, computed in numpy.
Say it“Log p of x is at least the expected log-likelihood of x given z, minus the KL of the cloud from the prior.”
Where the bound comes from, in three lines

Start from log p(x) = log ∫ p(x|z) p(z) dz, multiply and divide inside by q(z|x), and use Jensen’s inequality (the log of an average is at least the average of the log):

\[ \begin{aligned} \log p(\mathbf{x}) &= \log \mathbb{E}_{q}\Big[\tfrac{p(\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{z})\,p(\mathbf{z})}{q(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x})}\Big] \\ &\ge \mathbb{E}_{q}\big[\log p(\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{z})\big] - \mathrm{KL}(q \,\Vert\, p) \end{aligned} \]

The gap is exactly KL(q(z|x) ‖ p(z|x)), how far the encoder’s cloud is from the true posterior. A better encoder closes the gap; a better decoder raises log p(x) itself.

reconstruction (nats)
KL, the rate (nats)
loss: rec. + β × KL
−ELBO: rec. + KL

Why bother

Generating new digits

Here is the payoff. To make a digit nobody wrote, draw a code from the prior and decode it. With the VAE this works, because the KL term packed the training codes into exactly the region where the prior puts its samples. A plain autoencoder has no such promise: the most honest thing we can do is fit a Gaussian to its codes and sample from that, and some samples land in the gaps. How do we score a drawing? We measure the distance from each sample to the closest of the 500 real test digits the page carries, and compare with how close real digits are to each other. Draw new samples from each model, then turn the temperature τ down and up.

\[ \mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}\big(\mathbf{0},\ \tau^2 I\big), \qquad \mathbf{x}_{\text{new}} = g_\theta(\mathbf{z}) \]
Read it as: τ = 1 samples from the prior itself; τ < 1 stays near its centre (safer, more typical digits), τ > 1 explores the edges. What we show is the decoder’s probability for each pixel to be ink, the mean image; a strictly Bernoulli sample would sprinkle each pixel on or off at random and look speckled. For the plain autoencoder, z is drawn from a Gaussian with the mean and covariance of its training codes, scaled by τ.
Say it“Draw z from a normal with variance tau squared, and decode it.”
median distance to nearest real digit
same, for real digits (to each other)
samples as close as a typical real digit
samples far from every real digit

Real-world project

Project: a VAE that learned MNIST in two numbers

MNIST (LeCun, Cortes & Burges) holds 70,000 handwritten digits collected by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology from Census Bureau staff and high-school students, each centred in a 28×28 grid: 60,000 for training and 10,000 for testing, written by different people. We downloaded it from OpenML (mnist_784) and trained the VAE offline, in plain numpy: backpropagation written by hand (checked against finite differences), the reparameterisation trick, the Adam optimiser, batches of 128, 40 passes over the training set. Its weights are embedded in this page as 8-bit integers with one scale per output unit, and every number below that says “browser” is computed by your browser from those exact weights.

1 · The map and the manifold

Kingma and Welling’s best-known figure decodes a grid of codes to show the whole learned manifold at once. Each grid cell is the decoder’s drawing at one point of the prior’s quantile grid, decoded live. Hover either panel: the map shows where that cell lives, and its digits show who lives there.

4 · Checking the browser against numpy

The page carries the first 500 test digits (stored at 16 grey levels to keep the page small) and, for each, the one random ε that numpy used. Your browser encodes all 500, computes every KL and reconstruction term from the embedded weights, and compares them with numpy’s values for the same images, weights and ε.

The same model in numpy

import json, numpy as np

w = json.load(open("ae_vae_weights.json"))               # the int8 weights this page embeds
def deq(m): return (np.array(m["q"], np.int8).reshape(m["rows"], m["cols"]) * np.array(m["s"])).astype(np.float64)
W1, Wm, Wv, W3, W4 = (deq(w[k]) for k in ("W1", "Wm", "Wv", "W3", "W4"))
b1, bm, bv, b3, b4 = (np.array(w[k]) for k in ("b1", "bm", "bv", "b3", "b4"))
relu = lambda a: np.maximum(a, 0)
softplus = lambda a: np.maximum(a, 0) + np.log1p(np.exp(-np.abs(a)))

def encode(x):                       # x: (n, 784) in [0, 1]
    h = relu(x @ W1 + b1)
    return h @ Wm + bm, h @ Wv + bv  # mu, log sigma^2
def decode_logits(z): return relu(z @ W3 + b3) @ W4 + b4
def terms(x, eps):                   # one-sample reconstruction (nats) and exact KL (nats), per digit
    mu, lv = encode(x)
    z = mu + np.exp(0.5 * lv) * eps
    lg = decode_logits(z)
    rec = (softplus(lg) - x * lg).sum(1)                    # Bernoulli negative log-likelihood
    kl = 0.5 * (mu**2 + np.exp(lv) - lv - 1).sum(1)
    return rec, kl

D = np.load("mnist.npz"); X = D["X"].astype(np.float64) / 255; Xte = X[60000:]
x500 = np.round(Xte[:500] * 15) / 15                        # the page's 16-level copy
eps = np.array(w["eps500"]).reshape(500, 2)
rec, kl = terms(x500, eps)
print(f"first 500 (16 levels): rec {rec.mean():.4f}  KL {kl.mean():.4f}  -ELBO {rec.mean() + kl.mean():.4f}")
print("digit 0: mu", np.round(encode(x500[:1])[0][0], 6), " rec", round(rec[0], 6), " KL", round(kl[0], 6))
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); R, K = [], []
for s in range(10):                                          # 10 draws of eps per test digit
    r, k = terms(Xte, rng.standard_normal((10000, 2))); R.append(r); K.append(k)
R, K = np.mean(R, 0), np.mean(K, 0)
print(f"all 10,000 test digits: rec {R.mean():.3f}  KL {K.mean():.3f}  -ELBO {R.mean() + K.mean():.3f} nats")
first 500 (16 levels): rec 141.6463  KL 6.2298  -ELBO 147.8761
digit 0: mu [2.55879 1.55723]  rec 83.461406  KL 8.332846
all 10,000 test digits: rec 144.186  KL 6.231  -ELBO 150.417 nats

Wrap-up

Five lines to remember

  • An autoencoder is an encoder and a decoder trained to reproduce their own input through a narrow bottleneck; the bottleneck forces a compact code, and no labels are needed.
  • A linear autoencoder can only find the PCA subspace. Non-linear layers let a code follow curved structure: two learned numbers rebuild MNIST digits about as well as PCA does with six.
  • A plain autoencoder’s latent space is a map with gaps: interpolation and sampling cross ground the decoder never learned.
  • A VAE encodes each input as a Gaussian cloud q(z|x) and trains with the reparameterisation trick z = μ + σε, which gives low-variance gradients through the sampling step.
  • Its loss, reconstruction + KL(q ‖ N(0, I)), is minus the ELBO, a lower bound on log p(x); the KL term packs codes where the prior samples, so decoding z ~ N(0, I) generates new data. β trades sharpness against a tidy map.

Check your understanding

An autoencoder with a 1,000-number code on 784-pixel images reaches almost zero reconstruction error. Has it learned something useful?

Probably not: with a code wider than the input it can learn to copy the pixels straight through. A bottleneck (or another restriction, such as noise on the input in a denoising autoencoder, or a sparsity penalty) is what forces it to learn structure.

Why can’t a linear autoencoder beat PCA, however long you train it?

Its reconstruction VWx lies in a k-dimensional linear subspace, and among all such subspaces the top-k principal components leave the smallest squared error (the sum of the remaining eigenvalues). Gradient descent can at best reach that subspace.

What would happen to a VAE trained with the reconstruction term only, without the KL?

The encoder could shrink every σ towards zero and spread the μs apart, so the sampling noise stops mattering: it becomes a plain autoencoder, with gaps in the latent space, and samples from N(0, I) would often decode to nonsense.

Why does the encoder output log σ² rather than σ, and why write z = μ + σε instead of sampling z directly?

log σ² can be any real number, so no constraint is needed to keep σ positive. Writing z as μ + σε with ε ~ N(0, I) makes z a differentiable function of μ and σ, so backpropagation can compute the gradient directly, with far less variance than the score-function estimator.

A cloud has μ = (1, 0) and σ = (1, 0.5). What is its KL from N(0, I)?

½[(1 + 1 − 0 − 1) + (0 + 0.25 − ln 0.25 − 1)] = ½[1 + 0.636] ≈ 0.82 nats.
